subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: When did Edward the Confessor die, triggering the succession crisis of 1066?
options: 5 January 1066
14 October 1066
25 September 1066
25 December 1066
questions.explain: Edward the Confessor died childless on 5 January 1066, leaving a disputed succession.

questions.q: At which battle did Harold Godwinson defeat and kill the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada?
options: Stamford Bridge
Gate Fulford
Hastings
Ely
questions.explain: Harold destroyed Hardrada's invading army at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066.

questions.q: On what date was the Battle of Hastings fought?
options: 14 October 1066
25 September 1066
20 September 1066
25 December 1066
questions.explain: William defeated and killed Harold at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066.

questions.q: Why was Harold's army at a disadvantage at the Battle of Hastings?
options: They were exhausted after defeating Hardrada at Stamford Bridge and marching rapidly south
They had no foot soldiers at all
They greatly outnumbered William's forces
They fought entirely without a shield wall
questions.explain: Harold's men were tired after Stamford Bridge and a forced march of about 250 miles south to meet William.

questions.q: Who won the Battle of Gate Fulford on 20 September 1066?
options: Harald Hardrada and Tostig
Edwin and Morcar
William of Normandy
Harold Godwinson
questions.explain: The Norwegian force of Hardrada and Tostig defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar at Gate Fulford.

questions.q: Where and when was William crowned King of England?
options: Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066
Winchester Cathedral in October 1066
Canterbury Cathedral in 1070
Westminster Abbey on New Year's Day 1067
questions.explain: William was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day, 25 December 1066.

questions.q: Why did the Normans build motte and bailey castles across England?
options: To dominate and control the surrounding Anglo-Saxon population
To act as centres of trade and markets
To serve as monasteries for Norman monks
To store the Domesday Book records
questions.explain: Quickly built motte and bailey castles gave the Normans strongholds to intimidate and control local populations.

questions.q: A monk's chronicle describes villages burned, livestock killed and thousands starving across Yorkshire in the winter of 1069-70. Which event does this describe?
options: The Harrying of the North
The Revolt of the Earls
The siege of Ely
The Battle of Gate Fulford
questions.explain: In 1069-70 William laid waste to the north, destroying crops, livestock and villages to crush rebellion.

questions.q: A northern village is recorded as 'waste' (worthless) in the Domesday Book of 1086. What is the most likely reason?
options: It had been devastated during the Harrying of the North
It had been given to the Church
It had become a royal forest
It had been rebuilt as a castle
questions.explain: Many northern manors were still recorded as 'waste' in 1086 because of the destruction of the Harrying of the North.

questions.q: Which rebel leader led Anglo-Saxon resistance from a base in the Isle of Ely?
options: Hereward the Wake
Edgar Aetheling
Edwin of Mercia
Waltheof
questions.explain: Hereward the Wake led resistance from the marshy stronghold of Ely, which fell to William in 1071.

questions.q: The Revolt of the Earls (1075) is significant partly because it showed that...
options: opposition to William now included Norman lords, not just Anglo-Saxons
the Anglo-Saxon royal line had finally been restored
William had lost control of Normandy
the feudal system had been abolished
questions.explain: The revolt involved Norman and Breton earls, showing discontent had spread beyond conquered Anglo-Saxons.

questions.q: In which year was the Domesday Book compiled?
questions.explain: William ordered the Domesday survey, completed in 1086, to record landholding across England.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of the Domesday Book?
options: To record landholding and resources so the king could assess wealth and tax
To list all the castles built since 1066
To record the reforms of the Church
To provide a narrative history of the Norman conquest
questions.explain: Domesday recorded who held land and its value, helping William assess landholding, resources and taxation.

questions.q: Under the Norman feudal system, what did tenants-in-chief owe the king in return for their land?
options: A set number of knights for military service
A yearly payment of church tithes
Free labour on royal building projects
A fixed share of all crops grown
questions.explain: Tenants-in-chief held land directly from the king in exchange for providing an agreed quota of knights.

questions.q: William grants a loyal follower a large estate made up of many manors. Under the feudal system, the follower's chief obligation to the king is to...
options: provide an agreed number of knights when required
pay all his income directly to the Church
govern the whole county as sheriff
build a cathedral on his land
questions.explain: In return for land, a tenant-in-chief owed knight service, supplying knights for the king's army.

questions.q: What was the effect of Norman 'forest law'?
options: Large areas were reserved for royal hunting, with harsh penalties for breaking the rules
Peasants were given free access to hunt in royal woods
All forests were cleared to build castles
Monasteries were granted ownership of every forest
questions.explain: Forest law set aside land as royal hunting grounds, imposing severe punishments on ordinary people who broke it.

questions.q: Who did William appoint as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1070, replacing Stigand?
options: Lanfranc
Anselm
Odo of Bayeux
Ealdred
questions.explain: William replaced the discredited Stigand with the reformer Lanfranc as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1070.

questions.q: How did Lanfranc reform the English Church after 1070?
options: He replaced Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans and set up separate church courts
He closed all English monasteries
He removed the Pope's authority over England
He allowed priests far greater freedom to marry
questions.explain: Lanfranc appointed Norman bishops, tightened discipline and created separate church courts for religious matters.

questions.q: Under Lanfranc's reforms, a man accused of a moral or religious offence, such as breaking a Church rule, would now most likely be tried in...
options: a separate Church court
the king's own household court
the local manor court
a Norman military tribunal
questions.explain: Lanfranc established separate church courts to deal with religious and moral offences apart from royal courts.

questions.q: What was the impact of the Normans on English monasticism?
options: They revived and reformed monasteries, building new stone abbeys and imposing stricter discipline
They abolished monasteries and seized all their land
They left Anglo-Saxon monasteries completely unchanged
They banned Latin from all monastic learning
questions.explain: The Normans reformed and rebuilt monasteries in stone, bringing continental discipline and stricter observance.

specSource: AQA GCSE History (8145) specification; Norman England, c1066-c1100
